claims.text: Replacing a conventional EAM reference with an MLP trained on ab initio high-temperature liquid configurations will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in free-energy calculations of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method applies to both solid and liquid alloy states at or near their high melting temperatures.
An MLP, such as a neural-network or moment-tensor potential, can be trained on ab initio liquid configurations and used as the reference in a TOR-TILD-like thermodynamic-integration procedure.
The intervention is most applicable to refractory or complex high-entropy alloys near and above approximately 2000 K.
At these temperatures, the liquid exhibits a broad range of atomic configurations.
The MLP is designed to capture many-body interactions and diverse local atomic environments.
Capturing many-body interactions and diverse local environments produces a closer match between the MLP energy landscape and the ab initio target landscape.
Training on diverse ab initio liquid configurations enables the MLP to represent the many distinct atomic arrangements in the liquid.
Conventional EAM references are optimized for a narrower and more ordered configuration space than that sampled by the liquid.
The limited configuration space represented by an EAM reference causes discontinuities or mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
Using the liquid-trained MLP reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD's EAM reference.
The expected reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch is approximately 30–50%.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the fidelity and diversity of the MLP training data.
Existing TOR-TILD EAM references inadequately capture the variety of liquid configurations.
The anticipated improvement is limited to temperatures and compositions sufficiently represented in the MLP training data.
The benefit may diminish for atomic-size or bonding environments lying far outside the MLP training range.
The intervention can be tested by comparing EAM- and MLP-reference thermodynamic integration over temperatures spanning the solid-to-liquid transition in the same alloy.
Failure of the MLP reference to produce a statistically significant reduction exceeding 30% in path mismatch across the tested range would falsify the hypothesis.
